Our team uses Github for tracking items of work.

This project is called Station, and it is a Terraform module that allows for deployment of Application Landing Zones in Azure.

Station is meant to be called as a module, from a parent module. This means you need to refer to the `variables.tf` file (and other variable files) to understand the input to Station.

## Testing Terraform Code
We use Terraform's internal testing framework to test our Terraform code.

To run all Terraform tests, use the `terraform test` command. This will execute every test defined in the `tests/` directory.

To run a specific test file only, use the `-filter` flag with the path to the test file:

```bash
terraform test -filter=tests/<test_file_name>.tftest.hcl
```

Our tests are written per feature we support. When we write test, we configure minimum and maximum values for the configuration options. Look at `tests/application.tftest.hcl` for examples on minimum and maximum configurations.

When we write new tests, we follow a pattern, like this:
- Create a new test file in the `tests/` directory.
- Configure required providers at the top of the file (tfe, azuread, azurerm, etc.). See existing test files for examples.
- The first `run` blocks in each Station test file must always contain any setup code required for running the test: This setup is often necessary for the "main" test logic to work, especially when dynamic or environment-specific values are needed. For example, in `tests/application.tftest.hcl`, the test begins with a `run "setup" {...}` block that sources the `./tests/setup-common` directory. This directory provisions commonly used resources and outputs their values. These outputs are then referenced in the main `run` blocks of your test. Always use the outputs from such setup modules to provide dynamic or required values to your main test logic.
- Tests are written as `assert` blocks inside `run` blocks, which contain the actual test logic. You should validate that inputs are set correctly, outputs are as expected, and any other conditions that need to be met for the test to pass.
- Always try to expand an existing `run` block instead of creating a new one, unless the logic is significantly different or requires a separate setup. This helps maintain clarity and organization in the test files.
- In the "main" `run` block(s), you need to crete a new `variables` block with overrides for actual values generated by other "setup" blocks. This is necessary for many configuration options.
- Refer to `/variables.tf` and other files that contain the word `variables` in the root directory to understand the available variables and their expected values. 
- Refer to the actual logic in the root directory to understand the implementation details and how the variables are used. This is crucial for writing effective tests that accurately reflect the expected behavior of the Terraform code.
- Refer to the official documentation of Terraform and providers when writing new tests:
  - Terraform: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/docs
  - Terraform Testing Framework: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/tests
  - AzureAD Provider: https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/azuread/latest
  - AzureRM Provider: https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/azurerm
  - TFE Provider: https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/tfe/latest
- Ensure variables are placed correctly within the `variables` block.
- Try to use existing test files if asked to write new tests.

It is important to verify which available versions there are of azurerm, azuread and tfe providers, and refer to the documentation to understand available attributes.

The structure of the repository is as follows:
- Root directory: Main module logic, provider resources may be defined here or calls to bigger child-modules (which can be found in the directories in the root directory).
- `tests/`: Contains all the test files. Each test file corresponds to a specific feature

When asked to write a test, please follow the above guidelines and ensure that the test is comprehensive, covering all necessary aspects of the feature being tested. If you have any questions or need clarification on specific parts of the code or testing framework, feel free to ask.
